docs.title: LiteALPR: Lightweight & Accurate License Plate Recognition
docs.text: Representative license plate samples across diverse layouts and visual conditions evaluated in LiteALPR.

docs.title: What is LiteALPR?
docs.text:
LiteALPR is an open-source, lightweight two-stage Automatic License Plate Recognition (ALPR) library designed for high-throughput workstation processing and resource-constrained edge deployment.

LiteALPR integrates two task-specific lightweight adaptations:

  1. YOLOv8n-Efficient Detector: Replaces dense C2f bottlenecks across backbone stages (P3–P5) and the PANet neck with lightweight C3Ghost modules (\(5 \times 5\) depthwise convolutions), reducing parameters to 2.00M, cutting \(416 \times 416\) compute to 2.36 GFLOPs (-30.8%), and accelerating CPU detection by 2.34× while preserving localization precision (99.45% \(\text{mAP}_{50}\), 88.07% \(\text{mAP}_{50-95}\)).
  2. SVTR26-Tiny Recognizer: Replaces 2D self- and cross-attention decoders with an attention-free Efficient RCTC Decoder using Height-wise Average Pooling (HAP) and 4-bucket aspect-ratio resizing (\(64 \times 64\), \(48 \times 96\), \(40 \times 112\), \(32 \times 128\)), reducing parameters to 4.22M and lowering latency to ~5.03 ms on GPU and ~8.32 ms on CPU.
  3. Multi-National Training & Degradation Modeling: Trained with Gaussian/motion blur, JPEG compression, additive noise, and PARSeq-style augmentations across Brazilian, Chinese, and Vietnamese/auxiliary benchmarks.

docs.title: Key Highlights
docs.text:
• ⚡ High Throughput: 66.45 FPS on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 GPU, 23.44 FPS on an AMD Ryzen 5 4600G CPU, and 15.70 FPS (10W) / 10.74 FPS (5W) sustained without thermal throttling on an NVIDIA Jetson Nano (4GB).
  • 🎯 Competitive Accuracy: 77.55% end-to-end exact-match accuracy (6.22% CER) on 5,230 full-scene holdout images (compared to 39.67% for out-of-the-box fast-alpr), and 89.14% sequence accuracy (3.28% CER) across 25,000 localized plate crops (87.96% on the 22,350 real-image crops; 89.25% on 20,036 strictly unseen-plate crops).
  • 📦 Plug-and-Play Python API: Simple LiteALPR() interface with automatic Hugging Face weight caching and modular detect() / recognize() execution.
  • 🔄 Flexible Backends: Native support for ONNX Runtime (CPU & CUDA), PyTorch (.pt / .pth), and TensorRT 4-profile static engines on Jetson Nano.
  • 🌐 Multi-National Benchmarks: Evaluated across Brazil (RodoSol-ALPR), China (CCPD) & CBLPRD-330k, Vietnam, and Auxiliary European subsets, with full sample-level split manifests in manifests/.

docs.title: Quick Example
docs.text:
from litealpr import LiteALPR

# Initialize pipeline (auto-downloads pre-trained models from HuggingFace)
model = LiteALPR()

# Read license plate
results = model.read("sample.jpg")

for res in results:
    print(f"Plate: {res['text']} | Confidence: {res['score']:.4f} | Box: {res['box']}")

docs.title: Benchmarks & Experimental Results
docs.text:
LiteALPR was trained and evaluated on two task-specific corpora spanning three regional groups:

  • Brazil (RodoSol-ALPR): 20,000 scenes (detection) and 20,000 crops (recognition)
  • China: 20,644 CCPD scenes (detection) and 20,000 CBLPRD-330k crops (recognition)
  • Vietnam & Auxiliary: 11,651 scenes (detection) and 12,595 crops (recognition: 4,556 public Vietnamese, 5,547 synthetic Vietnamese, 1,036 self-collected Vietnamese, and 1,456 auxiliary European crops)

docs.title: Dataset Splits Summary
docs.text:
Task / Partition Brazil China Vietnam & Aux. Total Full-Image Plate Detection (Scenes) 20,000 20,644 11,651 52,295 Training 15,990 16,502 9,344 41,836 Validation 1,999 2,038 1,192 5,229 Testing 2,011 2,104 1,115 5,230 Cropped Character Recognition (Crops) 20,000 20,000 12,595 52,595 Training 9,454 9,570 5,976 25,000 Validation 986 980 629 2,595 Testing 9,560 9,450 5,990 25,000
  • Plates per scene (Detection test, 5,230 scenes): 5,156 single-plate (98.59%) and 74 multi-plate (1.41%: 52 with 2, 16 with 3, 4 with 4, and 2 with 5 plates).
  • End-to-End Holdout Set (5,230 full-scene images): Distinct from the detection test split; combines 3,981 detection-test scenes having verified character labels (2,104 ccpd_test, 1,742 rodosol_test, 135 vn_test) with 1,249 additional ccpd_extra scenes strictly disjoint from detector training/validation.
  • Reproducible Split Manifests: Provided in manifests/ (detection_split_manifest.csv, ocr_split_manifest.csv with unseen_plate flag, and e2e_holdout_manifest.csv).

Benchmarking Protocol

Workstation benchmarks run in ONNX FP32 precision (\(N=1\) batch size, \(416 \times 416\) detector deployment resolution, 50 warm-up runs discarded, explicit cudaDeviceSynchronize() barriers on GPU, and 6 intra-op CPU threads on the AMD Ryzen 5 4600G). Latency (\(\text{mean} \pm \text{std}\)) is measured per-image over 1,000 samples, while FPS standard deviation is computed across 5 consecutive 1,000-image passes.

docs.title: 1. End-to-End Pipeline Performance
docs.text:
Full-pipeline latency, throughput, exact-match accuracy (E2E Acc.), and Character Error Rate (E2E CER) on the 5,230-scene holdout set (missed detections with \(\text{IoU} < 0.50\) count as full-length CER deletions):

Platform Model / Pipeline Params Pre (ms) Infer (ms) Post (ms) Total (ms) FPS E2E Acc. (%) E2E CER (%) GPU (RTX 3060 12GB) fast-alpr (out-of-the-box) 2.68M 4.58 ± 0.85 15.06 ± 3.27 5.62 ± 2.96 25.27 ± 5.67 39.57 ± 4.30 39.67 34.79 YOLOv8n + SVTRv2-Tiny (Baseline) 8.12M 1.54 ± 0.41 12.38 ± 2.43 1.55 ± 0.20 15.84 ± 2.79 63.13 ± 0.70 78.60 5.60 LiteALPR (Ours) 6.22M 1.63 ± 0.40 11.57 ± 5.87 1.49 ± 0.12 15.05 ± 6.01 66.45 ± 1.80 77.55 6.22 CPU (Ryzen 5 4600G) fast-alpr (out-of-the-box) 2.68M 5.10 ± 1.18 24.02 ± 3.29 4.17 ± 2.44 33.30 ± 4.92 30.03 ± 0.80 39.67 34.79 YOLOv8n + SVTRv2-Tiny (Baseline) 8.12M 5.26 ± 3.55 58.53 ± 13.50 0.95 ± 0.78 65.08 ± 14.28 15.37 ± 0.30 78.60 5.60 LiteALPR (Ours) 6.22M 6.52 ± 3.99 34.04 ± 9.32 1.80 ± 2.06 42.67 ± 8.66 23.44 ± 0.20 77.55 6.22

docs.title: Per-Subset End-to-End Breakdown (4-Bucket Resizing)
docs.text:
Holdout Subset Scenes Baseline (%) LiteALPR (%) Standard Chinese (ccpd_extra) 1,249 96.80 94.72 Brazilian (rodosol_test) 1,742 88.29 87.43 Vietnamese (vn_test) 135 73.33 81.48 Tilted/Blurred Chinese (ccpd_test) 2,104 60.12 58.94 Overall (E2E Acc. / CER) 5,230 78.60 / 5.60 77.55 / 6.22

Key Takeaway: Against the domain-matched 4-bucket baseline (YOLOv8n + SVTRv2-Tiny, 8.12M params), LiteALPR reduces parameters by 23.4% (6.22M) and speeds up inference by 52.5% on CPU (23.44 vs. 15.37 FPS) and 5.3% on GPU (66.45 vs. 63.13 FPS), trailing the baseline by 1.05 percentage points in overall E2E accuracy (99.90% detection recall, 16 FPs). Heavily tilted/blurred CCPD scenes (ccpd_test, 58.94%) account for most of the gap between full-pipeline E2E (77.55%) and ground-truth crop OCR (89.14%). Out-of-the-box fast-alpr (2.68M params, 2.79 GFLOPs) is smaller and faster on CPU (30.03 FPS) but reaches 39.67% E2E accuracy without domain adaptation.

  --rec_model pretrained_models/rec/svtr26_tiny/best.onnx

docs.title: 2. Detection Module Ablation (YOLOv8n-Efficient)
docs.text:
Models were trained at \(640 \times 640\); all evaluation metrics (GFLOPs, ONNX latency over 1,000 samples with 50 warm-up runs, and mAP over 3 random seeds on the 5,230-image test set) are measured uniformly at the \(416 \times 416\) deployment resolution ("Head" follows Ultralytics YAML terminology for the PANet neck and detection layers):

Configuration Params (M) GFLOPs (\(416\times416\)) GPU Lat. (ms) CPU Lat. (ms) \(\text{mAP}_{50}\) (%) \(\text{mAP}_{50-95}\) (%) Baseline YOLOv8n 3.01 3.41 10.02 ± 1.29 40.92 ± 5.44 99.44 ± 0.03 88.01 ± 0.11 Head (C3Ghost) 2.52 2.99 9.54 ± 1.24 19.69 ± 4.26 99.43 ± 0.06 88.98 ± 0.14 Backbone (C3Ghost) 2.49 2.78 9.04 ± 0.51 19.59 ± 3.38 99.44 ± 0.02 88.60 ± 0.12 YOLOv8n-Efficient (Ours) 2.00 2.36 9.02 ± 0.98 17.45 ± 1.62 99.45 ± 0.03 88.07 ± 0.12

Replacing C2f with C3Ghost across both backbone and neck reduces \(416 \times 416\) compute by 30.8% (\(3.41 \rightarrow 2.36\) GFLOPs), cuts parameters by 33.6% (\(3.01\text{M} \rightarrow 2.00\text{M}\)), and delivers a 2.34× CPU speedup (\(40.92 \rightarrow 17.45\) ms) while matching the baseline in \(\text{mAP}_{50}\) (99.45%) and \(\text{mAP}_{50-95}\) (88.07%).

docs.title: 3. Recognition Module Ablation (SVTR26-Tiny)
docs.text:
Impact of pruning 2D attention in favor of the Efficient RCTC Decoder (Height-wise Average Pooling) and synthetic degradation augmentations (latency measured over 1,000 samples with 50 warm-up runs; accuracy and CER over 3 random seeds):

Decoder Architecture Synthetic Aug. Params (M) GPU Lat. (ms) CPU Lat. (ms) Accuracy (%) CER (%) Baseline (2D Attention) No 5.11 5.55 ± 0.92 10.97 ± 1.26 86.72 ± 0.12 4.13 ± 0.09 Baseline (2D Attention) Yes 5.11 5.85 ± 0.89 10.84 ± 0.76 88.48 ± 0.11 3.46 ± 0.06 w/o Self-Attention No 4.33 5.95 ± 1.16 9.79 ± 0.74 85.98 ± 0.15 4.29 ± 0.11 w/o Self-Attention Yes 4.33 5.58 ± 0.77 9.81 ± 0.73 88.52 ± 0.12 3.48 ± 0.05 Efficient RCTC (Ours) No 4.22 5.29 ± 1.19 9.05 ± 1.34 86.55 ± 0.09 4.16 ± 0.06 Efficient RCTC (Ours) Yes 4.22 5.03 ± 0.51 8.32 ± 0.98 89.14 ± 0.10 3.28 ± 0.04

Overall across the 25,000 test crops, SVTR26-Tiny attains 89.14% sequence accuracy (3.28% CER), or 87.96% across the 22,350 real-image crops when excluding the 2,650 synthetic Vietnamese samples.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: LiteALPR is distributed via PyPI and supports Python 3.8 through 3.12 across Windows, Linux, and macOS.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
You can install LiteALPR easily with pip. Choose the option that fits your deployment target:

Standard (Auto-detect)CPU (ONNX) InferenceNVIDIA GPU (ONNX) AccelerationFrom Source 

pip install litealpr
LiteALPR will automatically detect available acceleration hardware and run with default CPU/GPU fallbacks.

pip install litealpr[cpu]
Installs standard onnxruntime for optimal lightweight CPU inference.

pip install litealpr[gpu]
Installs onnxruntime-gpu for CUDA execution provider acceleration on NVIDIA GPUs.

git clone https://github.com/vn-anhnth/LiteALPR.git
cd LiteALPR
pip install -e .

docs.title: Automatic Model Downloads
docs.text:
When you first instantiate LiteALPR() in your code:

from litealpr import LiteALPR

model = LiteALPR()

LiteALPR checks your local cache directory (~/.cache/huggingface/hub/ or custom paths) for the official ONNX models. If they are not found, it automatically downloads the latest models from our Hugging Face repository:

  • Detection Model: yolov8n_efficient/best_416.onnx (~8.1 MB)
  • Recognition Model: svtr26_tiny/best.onnx (~17.0 MB)

You do not need to download or place model files manually!

docs.title: Edge Deployment (Jetson Nano)
docs.text: To demonstrate the viability of LiteALPR on resource-constrained edge hardware, we deployed and profiled the pipeline on an embedded NVIDIA Jetson Nano (4GB) using TensorRT 8.2.1.

docs.title: Hardware & Software Specifications
docs.text:
• Hardware: NVIDIA Jetson Nano Developer Kit (4GB)
    • CPU: Quad-core ARM Cortex-A57
    • GPU: 128-core NVIDIA Maxwell (GM20B)
    • Memory: 4 GB 64-bit LPDDR4 (25.6 GB/s bandwidth)
    • Configured Power Modes: 10W MAXN (nvpmodel -m 0) and 5W (nvpmodel -m 1)
  • Software Environment:
    • OS: Ubuntu 18.04 (JetPack 4.6.1)
    • CUDA / cuDNN: CUDA 10.2 / cuDNN 8.2
    • TensorRT: 8.2.1
    • Python: 3.6.9

docs.title: Step 1: Export Models to ONNX
docs.text:
Export the trained PyTorch models to ONNX on your host workstation:

# Export Detection Model (416x416)
python tools/export_det.py \
    -m output/det/yolov8n_efficient/train/weights/best.pt \
    --imgsz 416 \
    --opset 12

# Export Recognition Model (dynamic input shapes)
python tools/export_rec.py \
    -m output/rec/svtr26_tiny/train/best.pth \
    --save_path output/rec/svtr26_tiny/train/best.onnx \
    --opset 12 \
    --dynamic

docs.title: Step 2: Calibrate INT8 & Build 4-Profile TensorRT Engines
docs.text:
Because TensorRT 8.2.1 exhibits numerical divergence when compiling multi-aspect-ratio transformers under a single dynamic profile, SVTR26-Tiny is compiled with four static optimization profiles matching its discrete aspect-ratio buckets (64×64, 48×96, 40×112, and 32×128). INT8 Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) uses IInt8EntropyCalibrator2 calibrated on 500 validation crops strictly disjoint from the 25,000-crop test set.

# 1. Build YOLOv8n-Efficient Detector Engine (FP16 at 416x416)
/usr/src/tensorrt/bin/trtexec --onnx=pretrained_models/det/yolov8n_efficient/best_416.onnx \
    --saveEngine=yolov8n_efficient_416_fp16.engine \
    --fp16 \
    --workspace=1024

# 2. Generate INT8 Entropy Calibration Cache (500 validation crops)
python test_performance/build_int8_calib.py \
    --onnx pretrained_models/rec/svtr26_tiny/best.onnx \
    --calib-out svtr26_tiny.calib \
    --labels-file dataset/rec/val_labels.txt \
    --dataset-dir dataset/rec \
    --num-images 500

# 3. Compile 4-Profile Static Recognizer Engines (FP32, FP16, and INT8)
python test_performance/build_trt_4profiles.py \
    --onnx pretrained_models/rec/svtr26_tiny/best.onnx \
    --calib svtr26_tiny.calib \
    --precision all \
    --output-dir .

docs.title: Step 3: Standalone Latency & Precision Trade-offs
docs.text:
Pure GPU inference latency was measured in 10W MAXN mode (nvpmodel -m 0) over 1,000 iterations (with 100 warm-up runs). At \(416 \times 416\), YOLOv8n-Efficient (FP16) achieves 20.66 ms detection latency. Across the full 25,000-crop test set, SVTR26-Tiny precision trade-offs (latency measured at \(32 \times 128\)) are:

Precision Engine Size Pure GPU Latency (ms) Test Accuracy (%) Test CER (%) FP32 141 MB 23.05 89.14 3.28 FP16 129 MB 23.50 89.14 3.28 INT8 (PTQ) 44 MB 27.06 89.12 3.29

Hardware Note: Both FP32 and FP16 TensorRT engines match the workstation PyTorch accuracy (89.14%). Because the Jetson Nano's Maxwell GPU (GM20B) lacks native INT8 Tensor Cores, INT8 PTQ introduces a ~4 ms reformatting overhead rather than a speedup, but shrinks serialized engine size by 3.2× (44 MB vs. 141 MB) with only a 0.02% accuracy difference (4 crops out of 25,000).

docs.title: Step 4: System Resource Monitoring (tegrastats)
docs.text:
Short-run (~1 min) system resource utilization in 10W MAXN mode monitored via tegrastats confirms that the complete pipeline peaks at 2.55 GB RAM, safely within the 4 GB limit:

Execution Phase RAM Utilization CPU Utilization GPU Utilization Temperature Idle 1,467 MB ~3% 0% 25.0°C Initialization 1,742 MB ~26% 99% 25.0°C Peak Inference 2,554 MB ~35% 40–99% 32.0°C Cooldown 1,467 MB ~22% 0% 30.5°C

(Initialization exhibits a brief 99% GPU spike during TensorRT engine deserialization before thermal inertia raises die temperature above 25.0°C.)

docs.title: Step 5: 30-Minute Always-On Thermal & Power Stress Testing
docs.text:
To validate sustained stability under continuous operation, run the Always-On stress test combining YOLOv8n-Efficient (FP16) and the 4-profile SVTR26-Tiny (INT8, 44 MB) engine:

python test_performance/run_stress_test_jetson_nano.py \
  --images_dir /path/to/your/dataset/images \
  --det_model_path yolov8n_efficient_416_fp16.engine \
  --rec_model_path svtr26_tiny_int8.engine \
  --dict_path litealpr/license_plate_dict.txt \
  --duration 30 \
  --output_csv run_stress_test_results.csv

Across continuous 30-minute runs, the pipeline sustains 15.70 ± 0.07 FPS under 10W MAXN mode (nvpmodel -m 0, reaching a steady peak of 44.5°C) and 10.74 ± 0.03 FPS under 5W mode (nvpmodel -m 1, reaching a steady peak of 39.0°C), with zero thermal throttling.

docs.title: Pipeline & Architecture
docs.text:
LiteALPR is structured as a modular two-stage sequential pipeline: Detection followed by Recognition. Both stages are adapted to minimize redundant computations for high-throughput and edge-oriented deployment.

➔ YOLOv8n-Efficient ➔ ➔ SVTR26-Tiny ➔ 59P289136

docs.title: 1. YOLOv8n-Efficient for Fast Detection
docs.text: The first stage localizes license plate bounding boxes from full-scene traffic frames.

docs.title: C3Ghost Integration
docs.text:
Standard YOLOv8 architectures rely on multi-layer C2f blocks containing dense \(3 \times 3\) Bottlenecks across both backbone and neck. LiteALPR replaces C2f blocks across backbone stages (P3, P4, P5) and the PANet neck with lightweight C3Ghost blocks based on GhostNet:

  1. Intrinsic Feature Generation: Given input \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times H \times W}\), a primary \(1 \times 1\) convolution generates reduced intrinsic feature maps:

    \[Y' = X * W\]

  2. Ghost Feature Generation: Cheap \(5 \times 5\) depthwise convolutions (\(\Phi\)) synthesize remaining feature maps from each intrinsic channel:

    \[y_{ij} = \Phi_{i,j}(y'_i), \quad \forall i = 1, \dots, m; \quad j = 1, \dots, s\]

  3. Feature Concatenation: Intrinsic and ghost feature maps are concatenated along the channel dimension:

    \[Y = [Y', Y'']\]
Baseline: Standard C2f Block Proposed: Lightweight C3Ghost Block

docs.title: Key Improvements (Evaluated at \(416 \times 416\) Deployment Resolution)
docs.text:
• Reduces parameters from 3.01M to 2.00M (33.6% reduction).
  • Reduces compute at \(416 \times 416\) from 3.41 GFLOPs to 2.36 GFLOPs (30.8% reduction).
  • Latency on NVIDIA RTX 3060: 9.02 ± 0.98 ms (vs. 10.02 ± 1.29 ms baseline).
  • Latency on AMD Ryzen 5 4600G CPU: 17.45 ± 1.62 ms (vs. 40.92 ± 5.44 ms baseline, 2.34× faster).
  • Preserves localization precision: 99.45% \(\text{mAP}_{50}\) and 88.07% \(\text{mAP}_{50-95}\) (vs. 99.44% and 88.01% baseline).

docs.title: 2. SVTR26-Tiny for Fast Recognition
docs.text: The second stage transcribes alphanumeric character sequences from cropped license plates (resized dynamically into four aspect-ratio buckets: \(64 \times 64\), \(48 \times 96\), \(40 \times 112\), and \(32 \times 128\) using PIL BICUBIC interpolation).

docs.title: Efficient RCTC Decoder (Height-wise Average Pooling)
docs.text:
General scene-text recognizers rely on heavy 2D multi-head self-attention and cross-attention decoders to handle curved or irregular text. Exploiting the predominantly horizontal geometry of license plates, SVTR26-Tiny prunes the 2D attention layers of SVTRv2's RCTC decoder and introduces the Efficient RCTC Decoder:

  1. Channel Fusion (\(1 \times 1\) Conv): Compresses incoming 2D features \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times H \times W}\) to \(X_{\text{fused}} \in \mathbb{R}^{128 \times H \times W}\).

  2. Height-wise Average Pooling: Collapses the vertical dimension \(H\) without learnable parameters to form a 1D horizontal sequence:

    \[X_{\text{pool}} = \frac{1}{H}\sum_{i=1}^{H} X_{\text{fused}}[:, i, :] \quad \in \mathbb{R}^{128 \times W}\]

  3. Linear CTC Projection: Maps the 1D sequence directly to the 38-token character vocabulary via CTC greedy decoding:

    \[P = \text{Softmax}(W_{\text{linear}} X_{\text{pool}} + b_{\text{linear}}) \quad \in \mathbb{R}^{38 \times W}\]
Original: Attention RCTC Decoder Proposed: Efficient RCTC Decoder

docs.title: Benchmark Impact
docs.text:
• Model size: 4.22M parameters (down from 5.11M in SVTRv2-Tiny, 17.4% reduction).
  • Latency on NVIDIA RTX 3060: 5.03 ± 0.51 ms (vs. 5.85 ± 0.89 ms baseline).
  • Latency on AMD Ryzen 5 4600G CPU: 8.32 ± 0.98 ms (vs. 10.84 ± 0.76 ms baseline, 1.30× faster).
  • Sequence Accuracy (25,000 test crops): 89.14% with 3.28% CER (vs. 88.48% accuracy and 3.46% CER in baseline; 87.96% on the 22,350 real-image crops).

docs.title: Reference Environment
docs.text: The performance metrics and evaluations reported in the SoftwareX manuscript and this documentation were benchmarked on the following workstation and embedded platforms.

docs.title: Workstation Hardware Specifications
docs.text:
• CPU: AMD Ryzen 5 4600G with Radeon Graphics (6 physical cores, 12 threads, 3.7 GHz; benchmarked with 6 intra-op threads)
  • GPU: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 (12 GB VRAM)
  • RAM: 32 GB DDR4

docs.title: Workstation Software Environment
docs.text:
• Operating System: Windows 11 Pro (64-bit) / Ubuntu 22.04 LTS
  • Python: Python 3.8+ (tested on Python 3.8.10)
  • CUDA Toolkit: CUDA 11.8
  • Benchmark Runtime (Manuscript): PyTorch 2.1.0, ONNX Runtime 1.16.3
  • Pinned Lockfile (requirements.lock): torch==2.2.0+cu118, onnxruntime-gpu==1.17.1, onnxruntime==1.19.2, ultralytics==8.4.98

docs.title: Embedded Edge Platform (Jetson Nano)
docs.text:
• Hardware: NVIDIA Jetson Nano Developer Kit (4 GB LPDDR4, 128-core Maxwell GPU, Quad-core Cortex-A57)
  • Software: Ubuntu 18.04 (JetPack 4.6.1), CUDA 10.2, cuDNN 8.2, TensorRT 8.2.1, Python 3.6.9

docs.title: Dependency Lockfile
docs.text:
To reconstruct the pinned Python development environment, install from requirements.lock in the repository root:

pip install -r requirements.lock

docs.title: Training, Evaluation & Export Guide
docs.text: LiteALPR includes a modular suite of scripts under tools/ for preparing datasets, training custom detectors or recognizers, running evaluations, and exporting to optimized ONNX models.

docs.title: 0. Environment & Setup
docs.text:
Clone the repository and install all dependencies:

git clone https://github.com/vn-anhnth/LiteALPR.git
cd LiteALPR

# Choose based on your runtime environment:
pip install -r requirements.lock       # Exact reference environment for reproducibility
pip install -r requirements.txt        # CPU (ONNX) Inference
pip install -r requirements-gpu.txt    # NVIDIA GPU (ONNX) Acceleration

docs.title: 1. Model Weights Preparation
docs.text:
Before training (fine-tuning) or evaluation, download the official pre-trained weights from our Hugging Face repository and place them in pretrained_models/:

LiteALPR/
└── pretrained_models/
    ├── det/
    │   └── yolov8n_efficient/
    │       └── best.pt
    └── rec/
        └── svtr26_tiny/
            └── best.pth

You can download them using wget or curl:

# Download Detection pre-trained weights
wget -O pretrained_models/det/yolov8n_efficient/best.pt https://huggingface.co/anhone3/LiteALPR/resolve/main/yolov8n_efficient/best.pt

# Download Recognition pre-trained weights
wget -O pretrained_models/rec/svtr26_tiny/best.pth https://huggingface.co/anhone3/LiteALPR/resolve/main/svtr26_tiny/best.pth

docs.title: Detection Dataset
docs.text: Detection models use the standard YOLO dataset format (data.yaml pointing to image and label folders).

docs.title: Recognition Dataset (LMDB)
docs.text:
The recognition module requires datasets to be formatted into Lightning Memory-Mapped Databases (LMDB) for fast I/O access during training.

Generate the LMDB using our CLI script:

python tools/create_lmdb_dataset.py \
    --data_dir ./dataset/rec \
    --label_files train_labels.txt val_labels.txt test_labels.txt \
    --output_dir ./dataset/rec/lmdb_data

docs.title: 3. Training Models
docs.text: Before training, configure your dataset paths, batch sizes, and learning parameters:

docs.title: Train YOLOv8n-Efficient Detector
docs.text:
Configure your dataset paths, batch sizes, and training hyperparameters inside the Global: section of configs/det/yolov8/yolov8n_efficient.yml:

Global:
  pretrained_model: "pretrained_models/det/yolov8n_efficient/best.pt"  # or null to train from scratch
  data: "dataset/det/data.yaml"
  epochs: 50
  imgsz: 640
  batch: 256
  device: 0  # GPU ID (e.g. 0), or list for multi-GPU (e.g. [0, 1] or more)
  project: "output/det/yolov8n_efficient"
  workers: 8

Start training with the CLI:

# Single GPU training (set device: 0 in YAML)
python tools/train_det.py -c configs/det/yolov8/yolov8n_efficient.yml

# Multi-GPU training (set device to GPU IDs, e.g. [0, 1] or [0, 1, 2, 3] in configs/det/yolov8/yolov8n_efficient.yml)
python tools/train_det.py -c configs/det/yolov8/yolov8n_efficient.yml

docs.title: Train SVTR26-Tiny Recognizer
docs.text:
Configure your training hyperparameters in Global: and Train: sections of configs/rec/svtr26/svtr26_tiny.yml:

Global:
  device: gpu
  epoch_num: 150
  pretrained_model: "./pretrained_models/rec/svtr26_tiny/best.pth"  # or null to train from scratch
  output_dir: "./output/rec/svtr26_tiny/train"

Train:
  dataset:
    name: RatioDataSetTVResize
    data_dir_list: ['./dataset/rec/lmdb_data/train']
  sampler:
    first_bs: &bs 256             # Batch size per GPU
  loader:
    batch_size_per_card: *bs
    num_workers: 4

Eval:
  dataset:
    name: RatioDataSetTVResize
    data_dir_list: ['./dataset/rec/lmdb_data/val']

Start training with torchrun:

# Single GPU training
torchrun --nproc_per_node=1 tools/train_rec.py -c configs/rec/svtr26/svtr26_tiny.yml

# Multi-GPU training (e.g. set --nproc_per_node to number of GPUs, such as 2, 4, 8)
torchrun --nproc_per_node=2 tools/train_rec.py -c configs/rec/svtr26/svtr26_tiny.yml

Pre-trained Models (Fine-tuning)

By default, the training process will load pre-trained weights to speed up convergence. You can change the path or remove it to train from scratch:

  • For Detection: Edit the Global.pretrained_model field inside configs/det/yolov8/yolov8n_efficient.yml.
  • For Recognition: Edit the Global.pretrained_model field inside configs/rec/svtr26/svtr26_tiny.yml.

docs.title: 4. Evaluation (Validation)
docs.text: Evaluate your trained checkpoints on the validation set:

docs.title: Evaluate Detector
docs.text: python tools/eval_det.py -m output/det/yolov8n_efficient/train/weights/best.pt

docs.title: Evaluate Recognizer
docs.text:
python tools/eval_rec.py \
    -c configs/rec/svtr26/svtr26_tiny.yml \
    -m output/rec/svtr26_tiny/train/best.pth

docs.title: 5. Batch Inference
docs.text: Test your checkpoints directly on directories of images. Pass --save_log to persist prediction logs:

docs.title: Infer Detection
docs.text:
python tools/infer_det.py \
    -m output/det/yolov8n_efficient/train/weights/best.pt \
    -d dataset/det/test/images \
    --save_log

docs.title: Infer Recognition
docs.text:
python tools/infer_rec.py \
    -m output/rec/svtr26_tiny/train/best.pth \
    -d dataset/rec/test \
    --save_log

docs.title: 6. Exporting to ONNX
docs.text: Export your trained PyTorch models to the ONNX format for deployment in production environments (C++, C#, TensorRT, etc.). You can configure the ONNX operator set version via --opset (default: 12).

docs.title: Export Detector
docs.text:
The ONNX file will automatically be saved alongside the original .pt file (e.g. best_416.onnx):

python tools/export_det.py \
    -m output/det/yolov8n_efficient/train/weights/best.pt \
    --imgsz 416 \
    --opset 18

docs.title: Export Recognizer
docs.text:
If you need it to accept dynamic width images in production, include the --dynamic flag:

python tools/export_rec.py \
    -m output/rec/svtr26_tiny/train/best.pth \
    --save_path output/rec/svtr26_tiny/train/best.onnx \
    --opset 18 \
    --dynamic

docs.title: Python API & Usage Guide
docs.text: LiteALPR provides an intuitive Python interface with flexible options for full end-to-end recognition, detection-only, or recognition-only tasks.

docs.title: 1. End-to-End Pipeline
docs.text:
The primary entry point is the LiteALPR class.

from litealpr import LiteALPR

# 1. Automatic device selection (GPU if available, fallback to CPU)
alpr = LiteALPR()

# Or explicitly choose target device:
# alpr = LiteALPR(device="cpu")      # CPU (ONNX) Inference
# alpr = LiteALPR(device="cuda:0")   # NVIDIA GPU (ONNX) Acceleration

# 2. Process an image file or numpy array
results = alpr.read("test_car.jpg")

# 3. Inspect results
for item in results:
    text = item["text"]  # Predicted license plate string
    score = item["score"]  # Confidence score (float 0.0 - 1.0)
    box = item["box"]  # Bounding box coordinates [x1, y1, x2, y2]
    print(f"Plate: {text} (conf: {score:.3f}) at {box}")

docs.title: Return Format
docs.text:
alpr.read() returns a list of dictionaries, one for each detected license plate:

[{"text": "59P289136", "score": 0.9842, "box": [450, 320, 680, 410]}]

docs.title: 2. Detection Only
docs.text:
If your workflow only requires vehicle/plate bounding box localization:

from litealpr import LiteALPR

# Disable text recognition
alpr = LiteALPR(use_rec=False)

# Detect plates
boxes = alpr.detect("test_car.jpg")

for box in boxes:
    # box format: [x1, y1, x2, y2] (integer pixel coordinates)
    print("Detected box:", box)

docs.title: 3. Recognition Only
docs.text:
If you already have cropped license plate images (e.g., from an external detector or crop camera stream):

import cv2
from litealpr import LiteALPR

# Disable detection
alpr = LiteALPR(use_det=False)

# Pass either image path or loaded BGR numpy array
crop = cv2.imread("cropped_plate.jpg")
text, score = alpr.recognize(crop)

print(f"Plate Text: {text} | Confidence: {score:.4f}")

docs.title: 4. Custom Local Models & Backends
docs.text:
Note: To download the pre-trained .onnx weights manually for offline usage, you can fetch them directly from our Hugging Face repository.

LiteALPR automatically supports both ONNX Runtime and PyTorch checkpoints based on the file extension:

docs.title: Using ONNX Models (Recommended)
docs.text:
alpr = LiteALPR(
    det_model_path="path/to/custom_yolo.onnx",
    rec_model_path="path/to/custom_svtr.onnx",
    device="cuda:0",
)

docs.title: Using PyTorch Checkpoints
docs.text:
alpr = LiteALPR(
    det_model_path="path/to/weights/best.pt",
    rec_model_path="path/to/weights/best.pth",
    device="cuda:0",
)

docs.title: LiteALPR(...) Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Default Description det_model_path str | Path | None None Path to detection weights (.onnx or .pt). Auto-downloaded from HuggingFace if None. rec_model_path str | Path | None None Path to recognition weights (.onnx or .pth). Auto-downloaded from HuggingFace if None. use_det bool True Whether to enable the detection stage. Set to False for recognition-only mode. use_rec bool True Whether to enable the text recognition stage. Set to False for detection-only mode. device str | torch.device | None None Target execution device ("cuda:0", "cpu"). Defaults to "cuda:0" if CUDA is available, otherwise "cpu".

docs.title: Methods Summary
docs.text: Method Arguments Returns Description read(image, conf_thresh=0.25) image_path (str) or img (numpy array) List[Dict] Runs end-to-end detection and recognition. Returns list of {"box": [x1, y1, x2, y2], "text": str, "score": float}. detect(image, conf_thresh=0.25) image_path (str) or img (numpy array) List[List[int]] Runs detection stage only. Returns bounding boxes [[x1, y1, x2, y2], ...]. recognize(crop_img) image_path (str) or crop_img (numpy array) Tuple[str, float] Runs recognition stage on cropped plate. Returns (text, confidence).
